newsitem.title: SWEDEN: SAS Cargo sees better '97 after costs hit '96.
newsitem.headline: SAS Cargo sees better '97 after costs hit '96.

text.p: The freight operations of Scandinavian airline SAS were hit by costs and competition in 1996 but 1997 would be a better year, the division's managing director Peter Gronlund said on Wednesday.
SAS cargo operations contributed 300 million crowns less to the airline's bottom line profit than targeted.
"The budget was wrong. It was too optimistic," Gronlund told Reuters in an interview at the airline's headquarters in Sweden.
"We didn't gain the revenue we had expected in certain areas because of competition, pricing, etc. Our costs were a little bit over the budget in certain areas."
For the past couple of months traffic volumes have been good and 1997 would be a better year, Gronlund said.
"I believe we will be coming out a little better than in 1996," he said.
Last year, when SAS introduced its Boeing 747 freighter service once weekly to New York and twice weekly to the Far East, several other airlines also started Boeing 747 cargo operations from Sweden.
"If you look at the capacity situation in 1996 a number of carriers came in and capacity was almost doubled. So there might be too much capacity," Gronlund said.
Despite possible overcapacity on the ex-Sweden cargo market, Gronlund said the airline had no plans to end its Boeing 747 freighter operation.
"We are not pulling out. Whether the others will do so or not, I don't know," Gronlund said.
Asked if changing the schedule or route of the Boeing 747 operation was an option, Gronlund said: "We're looking into it."
Air cargo market analysts say it was unlikely if the Gothenburg-New York leg of the SAS freighter -- the airline's only all-cargo aircraft -- could be profitable.

The aircraft, which is leased from Atlas Inc. of the United States, flies between the Swedish west coast city of Gothenburg and Osaka/Macao two times per week and between Gothenburg and New York once a week.
He said a drive to improve quality, which included employing trouble-shooters to monitor operations on the ground, helped lift volumes.
"In 1996 we were not able to use our capacity 100 percent. It's going much better now and we are happy with how it's been going over the past couple months," Gronlund said.
"We were not satisfied with the quality that we had. We want to be a...high-quality carrier," Gronlund said.
"SAS succeeded in a number of ways to create a better product. This may be why we've been able to increase our volumes."
Last week the airline began a passenger flight between New York and Copenhagen five times weekly with a Boeing 767. "It will take approximately 15 tonnes of cargo," he said.
It was too early to say how the market had received this new service, Gronlund said.
Asked if it would be possible for the airline to increase rates in the next six months, Gronlund said no. But it said it could be possible sometime over the next year.
"I believe the market is quite competitive. So we haven't been speculating a lot on price increases," he said.
-- Abigail Schmelz, Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700-1003
